notes.text: The end — Of God's patience towards Israel, the end of their ripening, they are now fully ripe, fit to be gathered. Pass by them - God had with admirable patience spared, but now he will no more pardon or spare.
With silence — So great will be the cruelty of the enemy, that they dare not bury them, or if they do, it must be undiscerned.
To fail — Either to root them out, or to enslave them.

When — Ye that could wish there were nothing to interrupt your marketing, that look on solemn times of worship as burdensome, such was the first day of every month, and the weekly sabbath. Small - So the ephah being too little, the poor buyer had not his due. The shekel great - They weighed the money which they received, and had no more justice, than to make their shekel weight greater than the standard; so the poor were twice oppressed, had less than was their right, and paid more than they ought to pay.

That we may buy — They would have new moons and sabbaths over, that they might go to market to buy the poor. And when these poor owed but for a very little commodity, as suppose a pair of shoes, these merciless men would take the advantage against them, and make them sell themselves to pay the debt. The refuse - This was another kind of oppression, corrupted wares, sold to those that were necessitous.
Hath sworn — By himself. Forget - Suffer to pass unpunished.

The land — The people of it. For this - This that you have done, and this that God will do. And it - The judgment, the displeasure of God, shall rise and grow like a mighty wasting flood. It - The land. Drowned - As Egypt by the overflowing of the Nile.

At noon — So Israel's sun did as at noon set under the dark cloud of conspiracies and civil wars by Shallum, Menahem, Pekah, and Hosea, 'till the midnight darkness drew on by Pul, Tiglath- Pilneser, and Salmaneser. Darken - Bring a thick cloud of troubles and afflictions. In the clear day - When they think all is safe, sure, and well settled.

Upon all loins — All sorts of persons shall put on mourning. Baldness - Shaving the head and beard was a sign of the greatest sadness. A bitter day - A bitter day, which you shall wish you had never seen, shall succeed your dark night.
Shall wander — Search all places for a prophet or preacher, from the Mid-land sea to the dead sea, they shall search all corners for a prophet.
Continually — God is continually doing good: thou art continually doing mischief. O mighty - He speaks ironically. O valiant captain! To kill a few weak and unarmed persons.

Deviseth — Expresses what thy wicked mind had devised. Deceitfully - Doeg pretended only to vindicate himself from disloyalty, 1 Sam. xxii, 8, but he really intended to expose the priests, to the king's fury.

Pluck thee — Violently and suddenly as the Hebrew word signifies, from thy house and lands, and all the wages of thy righteousness. Root - Though thou seemest to have taken deep root, yet God shall pluck thee up by the very roots, and destroy thee both root and branch.
Fear — Reverence God's just judgment.
The house — In God's church, or among his people.

Thou hast — Destroyed mine and thine implacable enemies, and established me in the throne, of which I am no less assured, than if it were already done. I will continue in thy way, placing my whole confidence in thy power and goodness, and faithfulness. Before - In the presence of thy saints. David here describes the wickedness of mankind, nearly in the same words as in chap. xiv. To the chief musician upon Mahalath, Maschil, A psalm of David. Title of the psalm. Mahalath - This also seems to be the name of a musical instrument, or tune.

glossa.text:
*Doeg.* ((CASS.)) The adversary of David signifies Antichrist, who shall stir up the whole world; who shall come by signs and wonders before the coming of the judgment, and seeking help from Saul, that is, from the devil, shall announce that David, that is, Christ, has come into the house of Achimelech, that is, to the Church *Eccesiam*, which is the kingdom of the Father.

*Abimelech.* ((HIER.)) He says, in the Hebrew Achimelech, etc., *as far as* therefore Abimelech is the kingdom of my father, and it signifies the Jews.
*Why dost thou glory in malice,* etc. ((CASS.)) The first is an invective against Doeg, that he may strengthen the faithful against Antichrist and his accomplices.

*It hath devised. ((Ibid.))* A light mind, a headlong utterance: it does not think before it speaks, whence: *In the mouth of fools is their heart.* *stulorsorum*

*As a razor,* etc. ((Ibid.)) Which, while it promises renewal, cuts: so does that deceitful one, namely Antichrist, cut blessedness, and slay.
*Thou hast loved malice,* etc. ((CASS.)) He does not forsake evil who loves it above kindness; and if kindness touches his mind, he flees.
*A deceitful tongue. ((Ibid.))* That is, deceitful words, the ministers of falsehood, of men who bear one thing in the heart and bring forth another in the mouth.

*Therefore God.* ((CASS.)) Of the swift end of the wicked man. *And thy root out of the land of the living.* ((AUG.)) Our root is charity, etc., *as far as* for here is the dust which the wind drives from the face of the earth. ((Ibid.)) The root of evil is covetousness, which does not bring forth fruit in the land of the living. Or, he speaks of Antichrist, whose root is his ministers, who with him shall have nothing with the saints.

*The just shall see. ((Ibid.))* Derision for his casting down. *((Ibid.)) The just shall see.* What shall befall the wicked, etc., *as far as* because more than by all other evils he shall deceive the faithful .

*But I,* etc. ((Ibid.)) How the good man bears himself against him. ((CASS.)) Thus far the censure of that man; here the praise of the contrary part: behold a perfect demonstration. *A fruitful olive tree.* ((AUG.)) The people of God is an olive tree, from which the proud branches were broken off, that is, the Jews, and the wild olive of the Gentiles was grafted in. ((CASS.)) A fruitful olive tree, from whose shoot the Lord Christ came into flower, who was anointed with spiritual oil above his fellows.

*For ever and for ever and ever.* ((AUG.)) What he said *for ever,* he repeats *for ever and ever:* that by repeating he may confirm how firmly he is founded in the love of the kingdom of heaven.
*Thou hast done, and I will wait on thy name. ((Ibid.))* The things foretold, namely, that I am an olive tree, that I have hoped in mercy for ever.

notes.text: Who is — By describing the glory of Christ, and his preeminence over the highest angels, the apostle here lays a foundation for the reproof of all worshippers of angels. The image of the invisible God - Whom none can represent, but his only begotten Son; in his divine nature the invisible image, in his human the visible image, of the Father. The first begotten of every creature - That is, begotten before every creature; subsisting before all worlds, before all time, from all eternity.

For — This explains the latter part of the preceding verse. Through implies something prior to the particles by and for; so denoting the beginning, the progress, and the end. Him - This word, frequently repeated, signifies his supreme majesty, and excludes every creature. Were created all things that are in heaven - And heaven itself. But the inhabitants are named, because more noble than the house. Invisible - The several species of which are subjoined. Thrones are superior to dominions; principalities, to powers. Perhaps the two latter may express their office with regard to other creatures: the two former may refer to God, who maketh them his chariots, and, as it were, rideth upon their wings.

And he is before all things — It is not said, he was: he is from everlasting to everlasting. And by him all things consist - The original expression not only implies, that he sustains all things in being, but more directly, All things were and are compacted in him into one system. He is the cement, as well as support, of the universe. And is he less than the supreme God?

And — From the whole he now descends to the most eminent part, the church. He is the head of the church - Universal; the supreme and only head both of influence and of government to the whole body of believers. Who is - The repetition of the expression { Colossians i, 15} points out the entrance on a new paragraph. The beginning - Absolutely, the Eternal. The first begotten from the dead - From whose resurrection flows all the life, spiritual and eternal, of all his brethren. That in all things - Whether of nature or grace. He might have the preeminence - Who can sound this depth?
For it pleased the Father that all fulness — All the fulness of God. Should dwell in him - Constantly, as in a temple; and always ready for our approach to him.

Through the blood of the cross — The blood shed thereon. Whether things on earth - Here the enmity began: therefore this is mentioned first. Or things in heaven - Those who are now in paradise; the saints who died before Christ came.

And you that were alienated, and enemies — Actual alienation of affection makes habitual enmity. In your mind - Both your understanding and your affections. By wicked works - Which continually feed and increase inward alienation from, and enmity to, God. He hath now reconciled - From the moment ye believed.

By the body of his flesh — So distinguished from his body, the church. The body here denotes his entire manhood. Through death - Whereby he purchased the reconciliation which we receive by faith. To present you - The very end of that reconciliation. Holy - Toward God. Spotless - In yourselves. Unreprovable - As to your neighbour.

If ye continue in the faith — Otherwise, ye will lose all the blessings which ye have already begun to enjoy. And be not removed from the hope of the gospel - The glorious hope of perfect love. Which is preached - Is already begun to be preached to every creature under heaven.

Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you, and fill up — That is, whereby I fill up. That which is behind of the sufferings of Christ - That which remains to be suffered by his members. These are termed the sufferings of Christ,

1. Because the suffering of any member is the suffering of the whole; and of the head especially, which supplies strength, spirits, sense, and motion to all.

2. Because they are for his sake, for the testimony of his truth. And these also are necessary for the church; not to reconcile it to God, or satisfy for sin, (for that Christ did perfectly,) but for example to others, perfecting of the saints, and increasing their reward.
According to the dispensation of God which is given me — Or, the stewardship with which I am intrusted.
The mystery — Namely, Christ both justifying and sanctifying gentiles, as well as Jews. Which hath been comparatively hid from former ages and past generations of men.
Christ dwelling and reigning in you, The hope of glory — The ground of your hope.
We teach the ignorant, and admonish them that are already taught.

glossa.text: *Who is the image.* In one way the image of a king is in a coin, in another in a son. We are the coin, in whom the image of God is Christ the Son. No image of God ought to be worshipped, save that which is the very thing that he himself is, nor is that image to be worshipped instead of him, but with him.

*The head of the body, the Church.* Because he stands to the Church as the head to the body. And since the Church began from Abel, how is he their head? Rightly, because he is the beginning of the Church, that is, its founder. *Who is the beginning.* Of the Church according to the divinity, that is, the founder of the Church, because he has illumined all the just, who from Abel as far as the last just man are begotten, by the power of his divinity and by the gift of his mercy. According to the humanity also he can be called the beginning of the Church, because it is founded upon the faith of his humanity. And rightly is he himself head and beginning, and ruler, and founder, because he himself is the firstborn, etc. *The firstborn,* etc. As he was born before all things of God, that he might create all things, so as man he first rises again, that he may restore, that he may always be first and chief.
*The fulness.* Because he can do all things of himself; whence: *As the Father has life in himself, so also the Son, who raises up and quickens whom he will,* thus he is shown to be perfect God.

*To reconcile through him.* It pleased God to reconcile through him, and he himself made peace not gratuitously, but through blood, things heavenly and things earthly, whence entrance into heaven lies open to man. *All things,* made through him, live in him their author.
*Alienated and enemies* to his council, which comes to the same thing, because they did not receive the things which God commanded through Moses, inasmuch as they were devoted to their own idols.
*He has reconciled in the body.* If, mortal and dead, he was able to reconcile, now, immortal, he can do all things.

*If yet you continue.* Therefore he had said so many and so great things about Christ, that they themselves might place their hope in him alone, in whom are all things; that they might not think themselves to be made subject to any of the elements or of the angels: he alone is to be worshipped, and no one is to be reckoned in comparison with him. *In all.* Which new creature is now under heaven, yet is still a pilgrim, but nevertheless will come to glory.
*I fill up.* Those of the sufferings which Christ endured, or which he has now commanded to be endured, which are still lacking, I fill up, that is, I am ready to suffer.

*I am made.* He says that he was made a minister of the Gospel by God through Christ, that the ministry begun by God might be fulfilled through a fit servant, which was unknown from the ages. *It has been given to me.* That I may fulfil what God preordained concerning you, namely that you should be saved through the incarnation. This he says, lest salvation should seem not to have been promised to the Gentiles. Or, *to me it has been given among you,* for that which is sought from my own is as much as if it were sought from myself.

*Rebuking.* We rebuke the gainsayers and overcome them, and we teach the obedient. *In all wisdom.* True wisdom is when Christ is acknowledged. *That we may present,* etc. *In which.* As if he should say: To my labour God joins miracles for confirmation.

notes.text: Martha was encumbered — The Greek word properly signifies to be drawn different ways at the same time, and admirably expresses the situation of a mind, surrounded (as Martha's then was) with so many objects of care, that it hardly knows which to attend to first.
Martha, Martha — There is a peculiar spirit and tenderness in the repetition of the word: thou art careful, inwardly, and hurried, outwardly.
Mary hath chosen the good part — To save her soul. Reader, hast thou?

glossa.text: *It came to pass, as,* etc. A discourse having been held about the love of God and of neighbour, an example of both loves is set down, not so much in word alone as in the showing forth of work. For by these two sisters two spiritual lives are signified. By Martha, a devotion busy in works, by which we are joined to our neighbour in charity. By Mary, the religious intention of the mind upon the word of God, by which we sigh in the love of God. The active life gives bread, either bodily to one that hungers, or of doctrine to one that is ignorant; it corrects the erring, calls back the proud to humility, dispenses what is expedient for each. The contemplative holds fast the charity of God and of neighbour, but rests from outward action, cleaves to the desire of the Creator alone, and, all cares being trodden underfoot, burns to see the face of the Creator, and longs to be mingled with the citizens above, who rejoice in eternal incorruption in the sight of the Lord. *Into her house.* When Jesus enters into the house, the wicked life, even if once it had been there, flees away; there remain two innocent lives, the laborious and the leisured, and between them, in the midst, is the very fount of life.

*Sitting beside.* The more humbly she sits, the more abundantly does it fall. Water flows together into the valley from the swellings of the hill. Mary sits, because the contemplative life, the tumults of the vices being stilled, now enjoys the longed-for quiet of the mind in Christ. Martha stands, because the laborious active life sweats in the contest.

*But Martha.* Mary was intent on how she might be fed by the Lord; Martha was intent on how she might feed the Lord: the latter prepares a banquet for the Lord, in the Lord's banquet the former already takes her delight.

*And answering.* Mary does not answer, but, as one at leisure, commits her cause to the judge. For if she were preparing words to answer, she would slacken her intentness on hearing. *Martha, Martha.* The repetition is a token of love, or perhaps of an intention to admonish, that she might listen more attentively.

*But one thing is.* The one is set before the many. For the one is not from the many, but the many from the one; and yet many things are necessary to those who tend toward the one. *Mary the best.* Martha's part is not blamed, since it too is good, but Mary's part is praised, and why it is best is added below.

notes.text: The purposes of God's love concerning Sarah, ver. 9-15.

The purposes of God's wrath concerning Sodom. (1.) The discovery God made to Abraham of his design to destroy Sodom, ver. 16-22. (2.) The intercession Abraham made for Sodom, ver. 23-33.

1. This appearance of God to Abraham seems to have had in it more of freedom and familiarity, and less of grandeur and majesty, than those we have hitherto read of, and therefore more resembles that great visit which in the fulness of time the Son of God was to make to the world. He sat in the tent-door in the heat of the day - Not so much to repose himself, as to seek an opportunity of doing good, by giving entertainment to strangers.

2. And lo three men - These three men were three spiritual heavenly beings, now assuming human shapes, that they might be visible to Abraham, and conversable with him. Some think they were all three created angels; others, that one of them was the Son of God. He bowed himself towards the ground - Religion doth not destroy but improve good manners, and teaches us to honour all men.

Where is Sarah thy wife? — By naming her, they gave intimation to Abraham, that tho' they seemed strangers, yet they well knew him and his family: by enquiring after her, they shewed a kind concern for the family of one, whom they found respectful to them. And by speaking of her, she over-hearing it, they drew her to listen to what was farther to be said.
I will certainly return unto thee — And visit thee. God will return to those that bid him welcome.

glossa.text: « And the Lord appeared to him in the vale of Mambre. » ((ISID. in Gen. )) Abraham bears a threefold figure: the first, of the Saviour, who leaving his kindred came into the world; the second, of the Father, because he offered up his only Son; the third (which appears in this place), of the saints who received the coming of Christ with joy . The tabernacle of Abraham signifies Jerusalem, where in their season the prophets and the apostles dwelt, and Christ at his coming was received by them that believed, and by them that believed not was hanged upon the tree.

« Three men. » Three men announce the coming of Christ, whom two angels accompany, Moses according to some, and Elias; the one a lawgiver, who in the law showed the coming of the Lord: the other, who is to come at the end, to announce the second coming of Christ and to preach his Gospel. Whence, when the Lord was transfigured on the mountain, they are seen with him. « He saw three, and adored one, » showing namely the Saviour, whose coming he was awaiting. Whence: « Abraham saw my day and was glad ((Joan. VIII)). » For he foresaw the mystery of the sacrament to come. Whence he washed their feet, that he might show the purification of the laver that was to be at the end of the world; for the feet signify the last things.

« Whom when he had seen. » *((GREG., lib. IX Moral., c. 51.)) Morally.* Abraham ran to meet three angels, because the man and master of the house, that is, the spiritual understanding, ought in the knowledge of the Trinity to pass beyond the barriers of the flesh, and as it were to go out at the door of the lowest dwelling. Let the care of the flesh, which Sara signifies, not appear abroad for ostentation, but behind the man's back, that is, under the discretion of the spirit, intent upon necessary things alone, let it not know how to uncover itself shamelessly, but to govern itself modestly.

((Ibid., lib. XXVIII, c. 4)). Abraham could not have seen the angels, received them into his lodging and set food before them, unless they had taken a body out of air: for they would not appear, they would not take food, unless they had a solid body of a heavenly element. Nor is it strange that now they are called angels, now the Lord, because they are called angels who minister without, and the Lord is shown, who commands them within.

« But I will fetch. » He returns to the offices of hospitality, which can be shown even to angels, when they take a bodily form out of the elements: which Abraham understanding, adored the Godhead in unity, and ministered to the angelic dispensation in visible form.

« Three sata. » These things are said in the type of the Church, which out of the three parts of the world is gathered into the unity of faith, and as bread without leaven is baked by the fire of the Holy Ghost.

((STRAB.)) A satum is a kind of measure. Three sata signify the three sons of Noah, out of whom the whole race of men was sown abroad. Therefore the Church is signified, or the evangelical doctrine that is to be sown throughout the whole world, and to be multiplied in the three parts of the world, Asia, Africa and Europe.

« Three sata, » of which Sara makes the loaves baked under the ashes, signify the three sons of Noah, out of whom the whole race of men was born: who, believing in the divine Trinity, were sprinkled with the water of baptism through Sara, that is, the Church, and were brought together into the one bread of the body of Christ. These are the three sata of meal which the woman in the Gospel leavened: they are unleavened loaves, because without the leaven of malice, and the anguish [ *Al.,* rancore] of wickedness, and the fervour of perverse doctrine, the unity of believers ought to be.

« Baked under the ashes. » They are baked under the ashes, that being baked by the vapour of the Holy Ghost through repentance for their sins, they may be made food acceptable to God.

« A calf most tender. » The tender and fatted calf is the body of Christ, which for the salvation of the world was offered up upon the tree of the cross. This is the calf that is killed for the prodigal son.

« Butter and milk » he set before them with the flesh of the calf, because milk signifies the old law; whence I Cor. III: « Milk I gave you to drink, not meat, » etc. For he had delivered to them the commandment of the law, as milk pressed out of the breasts of the two tables, that is the testament of faith, because they could not yet take the solid meat of the evangelical doctrine. The most rich and fat butter is the evangelical testimony, which like oil is given to the faithful for a sign. He set the calf before them with milk and butter, because neither can the body of the Lord be without the milk of the law, nor this without the Gospel. And they sat under the tree in sign of the Lord's passion, whereof they are the preachers.

« Behold she is in the tabernacle, » etc. ((STRAB.)) Abraham is without with the angels, Sara is in the tabernacle: because it belongs to the strong and the learned to preach openly, to instruct by examples: to the weak and the unwise, to learn and to be subject.

«

And she shall have a son, » etc. God promises a son to the barren Sara, saying: About this time I will come; he signifies not the time, but the quality of his coming, since through the son promised again the faithful people was to be born. Whence Isa. LIV and Gal. IV: « Rejoice, thou barren, that travailest not, » etc.

« Which when she had heard, etc. ((AUG. Quaest in Gen. )) Sara is reproved because she laughed, and not Abraham, although he had laughed in like manner; because Abraham's laughter was of wonder, Sara's of doubt, which he could discern who knows the heart. Sara denies that she laughed, whereas she cannot be hidden from God, but perhaps she thought that they were men. But Abraham understood God, yet in rendering the offices of humanity, which are necessary only to weak flesh; it is strange: unless he first judged them men, but men in whom he understood God to speak, certain signs of the divine majesty appearing: as Scripture often testifies that God appeared in men, but afterward they knew that they had been angels.

notes.text: Who — Who shall so dwell in thy church here, as to dwell with thee forever in heaven?

Uprightly — Loving, and serving God, and loving his neighbour not in word only, but in truth; and this constantly. Worketh - Makes it his business to do justly, to give to every one his due, first to God, and then to men. Speaketh - His words and professions to God and men, agree with the thoughts and purposes of his heart.

He — He that doth not speak evil of his neighbour. neighbour - That is, any man. Nor taketh - Into his mouth, doth not raise it, neither spread or propagate it; or believe it without sufficient reason.

Vile — An ungodly man. honoureth - He highly esteems and loves them, though they be mean as to their worldly condition, and though they may differ from him in some opinions or practices of lesser moment. Sweareth - A promissory oath. Hurt - To his own damage. As if a man solemnly swear, that he will sell him such an estate at a price below the full worth; or that, he will give a poor man such a sum of money, which afterwards he finds inconvenient to him. Changeth not - His purpose, but continues firm and resolved to perform his promise.

To usury — In such a manner as is contrary to God's law: of which see otherwise, Exod. xxii, 25 Levit xxv, 36, 37, &c. Reward - Or, a bribe for him who hath a bad cause. Moved - He shall abide with God here, and when he dies be forever with the Lord. David professes his trust in God, his adherence to him and love of his people, ver. 1-3. His satisfaction in God, ver. 4-7. He speaks in the person of Christ, of Gods presence with him, of his resurrection and the glory that should follow, ver. 8-11. Michtam of David. Title of the psalm. Michtam - This seems to be a title belonging to the musick or the song, which, with the rest, is now lost and unknown. As David was both a member, and an eminent type, of Christ, he speaks of himself sometimes in the one and sometimes in the other capacity: and therefore having spoken of himself as a member of Christ, in the former part of the psalm, he proceeds to consider himself as a type of Christ, and being inspired by the holy Ghost: towards the close he speaks such things, as though they might be accommodated to himself in a very imperfect sense, yet could not properly, belong to any but to Christ, to whom therefore they are justly appropriated in the New Testament.

glossa.text: *He that. ((Ibid.))* The answer of the Lord, etc. *as far as* as Christ the lamb, without breaking of members, who properly entered the temple, not that he might be expiated like the rest, but without stain. *He worketh justice.* As when he cast out of the temple those that sold and bought.

*He that speaketh.* Here he follows it out more fully. Truth is when the thing is so as it is said: this Christ did properly. *In his heart,* who at times kept silence toward the unworthy who questioned him fraudulently. *He hath not wrought deceit.* Deceit is in the tongue, when one thing is said and another is in the breast. Or, *he hath not wrought deceit,* because all that he heard from the Father, without any addition or suppression, he made known to his neighbours, that is, to the disciples; to the Jews, his neighbours according to the flesh. *Nor hath he done evil to his neighbour.* But he prayed for them; he did not take up reproach against his neighbours, as is plain from this, that he did not tear Judas with a biting rebuke.

*To nothing,* etc. ((AUG.)) This is perfection, that the malignant one avail nothing in a man, and that this be in his sight, that is, that he know for certain that no one is malignant save he who turns from the Creator to created things. *The malignant one,* that is, the devil, is despised; as when he said: *Go back, Satan,* etc. On the contrary, *he glorifieth them that fear the Lord.* He swore, when he promised the apostles with most certain truth: *Now I will not call you servants, but friends.*

*He that sweareth to his neighbour,* etc. ((Ibid.)) These three things are not great, etc., *as far as* since in the conclusion above he set down a past tense, *he is brought to nothing.*

*Money.* Either it is earthly, which is utterly forbidden to be given out at usury, and which the Lord handed over to Judas to be paid out to the poor, not for usury. Or it is spiritual, which is commanded to be given out at usury, that is, preaching for the instructing of men. *And gifts against the innocent.* Christ does indeed receive gifts, as from the Magi, and daily devout offerings; but not against the innocent; rather he gave his soul for them. *He that doeth these things shall not be moved.* Behold the complete answer to the questioner: he does them (he says), that he may invite us to the act, not only to the singing of them. *He that doeth these things shall not be moved.* ((CASS.)) The conclusion. In like manner he that doeth these things shall rest on the mountain.

The first begotten from the dead - From whose resurrection flows all the life, spiritual and eternal, of all his brethren. That in all things - Whether of nature or grace. He might have the preeminence - Who can sound this depth?
For it pleased the Father that all fulness — All the fulness of God. Should dwell in him - Constantly, as in a temple; and always ready for our approach to him.

Through the blood of the cross — The blood shed thereon. Whether things on earth - Here the enmity began: therefore this is mentioned first. Or things in heaven - Those who are now in paradise; the saints who died before Christ came.

And you that were alienated, and enemies — Actual alienation of affection makes habitual enmity. In your mind - Both your understanding and your affections. By wicked works - Which continually feed and increase inward alienation from, and enmity to, God. He hath now reconciled - From the moment ye believed.

By the body of his flesh — So distinguished from his body, the church. The body here denotes his entire manhood. Through death - Whereby he purchased the reconciliation which we receive by faith. To present you - The very end of that reconciliation. Holy - Toward God. Spotless - In yourselves. Unreprovable - As to your neighbour.

If ye continue in the faith — Otherwise, ye will lose all the blessings which ye have already begun to enjoy. And be not removed from the hope of the gospel - The glorious hope of perfect love. Which is preached - Is already begun to be preached to every creature under heaven.

Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you, and fill up — That is, whereby I fill up. That which is behind of the sufferings of Christ - That which remains to be suffered by his members. These are termed the sufferings of Christ,

1. Because the suffering of any member is the suffering of the whole; and of the head especially, which supplies strength, spirits, sense, and motion to all.

2. Because they are for his sake, for the testimony of his truth. And these also are necessary for the church; not to reconcile it to God, or satisfy for sin, (for that Christ did perfectly,) but for example to others, perfecting of the saints, and increasing their reward.
According to the dispensation of God which is given me — Or, the stewardship with which I am intrusted.
The mystery — Namely, Christ both justifying and sanctifying gentiles, as well as Jews. Which hath been comparatively hid from former ages and past generations of men.
Christ dwelling and reigning in you, The hope of glory — The ground of your hope.
We teach the ignorant, and admonish them that are already taught.

glossa.text: *Who is the image.* In one way the image of a king is in a coin, in another in a son. We are the coin, in whom the image of God is Christ the Son. No image of God ought to be worshipped, save that which is the very thing that he himself is, nor is that image to be worshipped instead of him, but with him.

*The head of the body, the Church.* Because he stands to the Church as the head to the body. And since the Church began from Abel, how is he their head? Rightly, because he is the beginning of the Church, that is, its founder. *Who is the beginning.* Of the Church according to the divinity, that is, the founder of the Church, because he has illumined all the just, who from Abel as far as the last just man are begotten, by the power of his divinity and by the gift of his mercy. According to the humanity also he can be called the beginning of the Church, because it is founded upon the faith of his humanity. And rightly is he himself head and beginning, and ruler, and founder, because he himself is the firstborn, etc. *The firstborn,* etc. As he was born before all things of God, that he might create all things, so as man he first rises again, that he may restore, that he may always be first and chief.
*The fulness.* Because he can do all things of himself; whence: *As the Father has life in himself, so also the Son, who raises up and quickens whom he will,* thus he is shown to be perfect God.

*To reconcile through him.* It pleased God to reconcile through him, and he himself made peace not gratuitously, but through blood, things heavenly and things earthly, whence entrance into heaven lies open to man. *All things,* made through him, live in him their author.
*Alienated and enemies* to his council, which comes to the same thing, because they did not receive the things which God commanded through Moses, inasmuch as they were devoted to their own idols.
*He has reconciled in the body.* If, mortal and dead, he was able to reconcile, now, immortal, he can do all things.

*If yet you continue.* Therefore he had said so many and so great things about Christ, that they themselves might place their hope in him alone, in whom are all things; that they might not think themselves to be made subject to any of the elements or of the angels: he alone is to be worshipped, and no one is to be reckoned in comparison with him. *In all.* Which new creature is now under heaven, yet is still a pilgrim, but nevertheless will come to glory.
*I fill up.* Those of the sufferings which Christ endured, or which he has now commanded to be endured, which are still lacking, I fill up, that is, I am ready to suffer.

*I am made.* He says that he was made a minister of the Gospel by God through Christ, that the ministry begun by God might be fulfilled through a fit servant, which was unknown from the ages. *It has been given to me.* That I may fulfil what God preordained concerning you, namely that you should be saved through the incarnation. This he says, lest salvation should seem not to have been promised to the Gentiles. Or, *to me it has been given among you,* for that which is sought from my own is as much as if it were sought from myself.

*Rebuking.* We rebuke the gainsayers and overcome them, and we teach the obedient. *In all wisdom.* True wisdom is when Christ is acknowledged. *That we may present,* etc. *In which.* As if he should say: To my labour God joins miracles for confirmation.

notes.text: Martha was encumbered — The Greek word properly signifies to be drawn different ways at the same time, and admirably expresses the situation of a mind, surrounded (as Martha's then was) with so many objects of care, that it hardly knows which to attend to first.
Martha, Martha — There is a peculiar spirit and tenderness in the repetition of the word: thou art careful, inwardly, and hurried, outwardly.
Mary hath chosen the good part — To save her soul. Reader, hast thou?

glossa.text: *It came to pass, as,* etc. A discourse having been held about the love of God and of neighbour, an example of both loves is set down, not so much in word alone as in the showing forth of work. For by these two sisters two spiritual lives are signified. By Martha, a devotion busy in works, by which we are joined to our neighbour in charity. By Mary, the religious intention of the mind upon the word of God, by which we sigh in the love of God. The active life gives bread, either bodily to one that hungers, or of doctrine to one that is ignorant; it corrects the erring, calls back the proud to humility, dispenses what is expedient for each. The contemplative holds fast the charity of God and of neighbour, but rests from outward action, cleaves to the desire of the Creator alone, and, all cares being trodden underfoot, burns to see the face of the Creator, and longs to be mingled with the citizens above, who rejoice in eternal incorruption in the sight of the Lord. *Into her house.* When Jesus enters into the house, the wicked life, even if once it had been there, flees away; there remain two innocent lives, the laborious and the leisured, and between them, in the midst, is the very fount of life.

*Sitting beside.* The more humbly she sits, the more abundantly does it fall. Water flows together into the valley from the swellings of the hill. Mary sits, because the contemplative life, the tumults of the vices being stilled, now enjoys the longed-for quiet of the mind in Christ. Martha stands, because the laborious active life sweats in the contest.

*But Martha.* Mary was intent on how she might be fed by the Lord; Martha was intent on how she might feed the Lord: the latter prepares a banquet for the Lord, in the Lord's banquet the former already takes her delight.

*And answering.* Mary does not answer, but, as one at leisure, commits her cause to the judge. For if she were preparing words to answer, she would slacken her intentness on hearing. *Martha, Martha.* The repetition is a token of love, or perhaps of an intention to admonish, that she might listen more attentively.

*But one thing is.* The one is set before the many. For the one is not from the many, but the many from the one; and yet many things are necessary to those who tend toward the one. *Mary the best.* Martha's part is not blamed, since it too is good, but Mary's part is praised, and why it is best is added below.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Martha was busy with many things; Mary sat at the feet of the Lord.
One thing is needful; we have come to listen.
A famine is coming, not of bread, but of hearing the word of God.
Speak, Lord; do not let us go hungry.
Be still, and set the worry down.
We choose the better part, and it will not be taken away.
Come, sit at the feet of Jesus and worship.
We have come to hear. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Set down the dish towel, leave the kitchen for a moment, and come sit on the floor at the feet of Jesus, the way Mary did.
We have come to listen.
Martha is not wrong to work, but she is worried and distracted by so much — and one thing, only one, is needful.
We have come to listen.
Amos warns of a hunger worse than empty cupboards: a famine of the word, people staggering to find what God is saying.
We have come to listen.
So be still. Let the noise settle. The Lord is speaking, and this hour is the better part that will not be taken from you.
We have come to listen. Amen.

lines: Mary sat at the feet of the Lord.

Set down the worry and the many things.
We have come to listen.

We have come to listen.
Be still before Jesus and worship.
We have come to listen. Amen.
